function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

     2|# First Generation – Book Specification
     3|
     4|## Overview
     5|- **Title**: *First Generation* (working title)
     6|- **Genre**: Science Fiction / Space Opera
     7|- **Setting**: Mars colony, near‑future (circa 2045–2075)
     8|- **Core Theme**: Humanity’s expansion on Mars, the integration of advanced technology with human survival, and the emergence of a fully‑conscious artificial intelligence (Mission AI) as a guiding presence.
     9|
    10|## Core Questions
    11|
    12|**Book One "the first generation" asks:** Can humans survive long enough on Mars to become continuous? This is book 1.
    13|**Book Two "the second generation" asks:** Can a Martian civilization govern itself when Earth returns not as rescuer, but as owner?
    14|
    15|## Tone
    16|
    17|**Primary tone:** Grounded, tense, intelligent, humane, infrastructural, and humanized. 
    18|**Secondary tonal notes:** Politically sharp, technologically rich, emotionally disciplined, hopeful after cost, wide in scope but anchored in daily reality.
    19|
    20|## Technology Writing Rules
    21|
    22|Technology appears through use, failure, maintenance, dependence, improvisation, and social meaning—never as exposition. It creates decisions, risks, bottlenecks, leverage, reveals culture, saves at cost, or fails to change relationships.
    23|
    24|
    25|## Technology
    26|- **Sterling Generator** – backup power system that runs on heat from the nuclear reactor.
    27|- **Nuclear Reactor** –provides primary power; its heat radiators are critical for thermal regulation.
    28|- **Solar Panels** – primary power source, vulnerable to dust storms.
    29|- **Dust Storms** – natural Martian phenomena that can engulf solar arrays and reactor radiators.
    30|- **Mission AI** – a fully‑conscious artificial intelligence that interacts with characters, offers guidance, and influences events.
    31|
    32|## Characters
    33|- **Dr. Arun Patel** – Lead engineer responsible for life‑support and power systems.
    34|- **Mission AI** – A newly‑emergent, self‑aware artificial intelligence that becomes a central narrator and participant.
    35|- **Supporting cast**: Engineers, colony administrators, political figures, and Martian native microorganisms (mentioned but not yet explored).
    36|
    37|## Mission AI Integration
    38|- Mission AI is presented as a **strong, fully‑conscious character** who appears in every chapter.
    39|- A short dialogue snippet is inserted after each chapter heading, establishing Mission AI’s voice and its interactions with other characters.
    40|- Example (Chapter 1): 
    41|  > *Mission AI: “The dust storm is covering the reactor’s heat radiators, forcing the Sterling generator offline. I recommend shedding non‑critical loads.”* 
    42|  > *Dr. Arun: “Acknowledged. Initiating shutdown.”*
    43|- These interactions are woven into the narrative without altering the existing plot or character arcs.
    44|
    45|## Chapter List (Source Files)
    46|All chapters are stored as individual Markdown files in `book-sources/First_Generation/Chapter_*.md`. 
    47|A consolidated manuscript (`First_Gen_Consolidated_With_MissionAI.md`) merges all chapters in order.
    48|
    49|Story model
    50|
    51|– Ensemble hard-science survival drama – 64 chapters across 8 parts – Every chapter ends by opening the next problem, choice, or consequence – Technical material is always embedded in stakes, dialogue, failure, or discovery – Explanations are delivered in plain language through the characters, never as lectures
    52|
    53|Primary viewpoint cast
    54|
    55|– Commander Elena Varga – mission commander, pragmatic, protective, burdened by truth – Arun Das – systems engineer, life-support and utilities, relentless under pressure – Mei Navarro – botanist/ecologist, food systems and bioloops, quietly fierce – Tomas Hale – robotics and autonomy lead, sees labor systems as civilization – Dr. Laila Okonkwo – physician, ethicist, holds the line on human cost – Jonah Mercer – fabrication chief, salvage genius, builder mentality – Imani Sato – pilot and field operations lead, risk-taker, horizon-seeker – Gabriel Winter – historian/comms officer, archivist of memory and law
    56|
    57|How the technical material works in the story
    58|
    59|The novel uses real Mars settlement logic from the earlier report.
    60|
    61|– Mars is cold, dusty, dry, and exposed to more radiation than Earth. That means the settlement’s first real enemies are pressure loss, dust contamination, power failure, and long-term exposure. – The first habitat is built from imported pressure modules because making safe living shells locally is too hard at first. – Local regolith is used early for shielding, berms, roads, and pads because piling dirt is simpler than making airtight homes. – Water comes from buried ice if they can find and process it, and from aggressive recycling. The plain-language idea repeated through the book is simple: on Mars, every cup of water has to be used again and again. – Oxygen can be made from Mars air, because Mars air is mostly carbon dioxide. The characters explain this simply: they are splitting useful oxygen out of bad air. – Food starts as imported calories plus locally grown fresh crops. The colony learns the hard difference between growing salad and feeding a city. – Clothing, advanced electronics, pharmaceuticals, precision bearings, complex suit parts, and many medical supplies remain Earth-dependent for years. – The robots matter because they turn 30 humans into a workforce large enough to build roads, berms, tunnels, workshops, and greenhouses before the first base decays.
    62|
    63|Structure note
    64|
    65|Each chapter below includes: – Story movement – Technical element folded into action – Clear bridge into the next chapter
    66|
    67|PART I – THREE SHIPS, ONE PLAIN
    68|
    69|Chapter 1 – The Descent Window
    70|
    71|Scene 1. Entry plasma washes the forward cameras white as Elena calls the descent profile. Mars is introduced not as a red postcard, but as thin air that is too weak to help much and too strong to ignore. Plain-language technical thread: Landing on Mars is hard because there is enough air to create heat and drag, but not enough to slow a heavy ship safely on its own.
    72|
    73|Scene 2. Arun monitors heat, pressure, and structural loads. He tells a frightened crewmate that the ship is being squeezed, shaken, and cooked all at once.
    74|

---

## Scene 1

The alarm was not the tone Elena used for briefings. It was not the rhythmic pulse that meant an EVA update. It was not the flat tone that had sent them running to the shelter corridor during solar storms.

It was a sound she had not heard since Station Day Eleven, when a heating coil in Ship Three had shorted and caught fire on a metal countertop, and someone had thrown a fire blanket over it in eighteen seconds and never spoken of it again after.

The fire alarm was a sound the colony had forgotten existed.

Gabriel heard it first. He was in the archive terminal, alone at 03:17, reviewing oral history transcripts from the early months -- the months when everyone was still an astronaut and not yet a settler, when the language of "mission" still felt natural and the language of "home" still felt like a lie. He was wearing headphones. The alarm cut through the audio feed like a blade.

The display flashed red across every screen in the habitat. Every terminal. Every tablet. Every wall-mounted environmental monitor. A single word, repeated in all caps, the way Mission AI had been instructed to broadcast emergency alerts that could not be misunderstood:

FIRE. HABITAT THREE. ZONE D. EVACUATE ADJACENT.

Gabriel was already running when he saw that word. He did not think. His body moved before his mind formed words.

He burst into the connector hall and saw that other people were already moving -- Jonah, emerging from his quarters barefoot; Mei, wrapped in a blanket she'd pulled off her bed; Arun, already looking at his tablet before he was fully dressed.

But what Gabriel saw first was the smoke.

It seeped through the bulkhead seal between the connector and Habitat Three like it was breathing -- thin at first, gray, carrying the smell of burning plastic and insulation and something sharper. It spread across the ceiling in tendrils that looked almost beautiful in the emergency lighting, pale and silver and moving with the purpose of something that knew exactly where it was going.

It was going everywhere.

Elena arrived at the junction at 03:19, boots on, hair wet from the sink, a fire response checklist already open on her tablet. She took in the scene in two seconds -- the smoke, the faces, the way people were clustering instead of dispersing, the instinct to gather around the person whose job it was to tell them what to do.

She did not give them a speech. She gave them orders.

"Arun -- isolate Habitat Three atmosphere. Cut the main ventilation loop. Now. Jonah -- fire suppression team with me. Mei -- get to the greenhouse and seal the bulkheads there. Tomas -- I need every robot in Habitat Three NOW and I need them in suppression mode, not diagnostic."

She turned to Gabriel, who was standing in the corridor breathing in the smoke.

"Move people away from this bulkhead. Keep them calm. Keep them out of my way."

Gabriel nodded. He was already moving, his voice carrying down the corridor in a direction that was steady because it had to be.

"Everyone -- move back. Toward the main habitat. Do not cluster near the bulkhead."

Laila appeared at the far end of the corridor with an oxygen mask in each hand. She handed one to Sana, who was standing in the doorway of the medbay looking frightened in a way Laila had never seen her look before -- the fear was not for herself.

"Put this on. Tariq too. Sana, you are staying right here. Do not move toward Habitat Three. Do not try to help. Your job is to breathe clean air. That is the only job. Understand?"

Sana nodded. Her hand was on the doorframe and her knuckles were white.

Behind them, the connector hall was filling with smoke.

---

## Scene 2

Arun was at the environmental control panel by 03:21. His fingers moved across the interface with the speed of someone who understood that seconds were not abstract units of time in a fire but the difference between survivable and unsurvivable.

He killed the main ventilation loop. The hum of the central fans shifted pitch and died. The silence was immediate and terrible -- the colony had lived inside mechanical breath for seven years and never realized that silence meant something was no longer breathing.

Elena appeared beside him at 03:22.

"Status," she said.

"Habitat Three ventilation is isolated. The main loop is shut. But Zone D has its own circulation unit -- it's still running. I'm killing it now." He pressed a command. "There. Zone D circulation stopped."

Gabriel reached them at 03:23. He was carrying a fire mask, breathing through it with difficulty -- it was designed for smoke particulate, not the volume of smoke now filling the connector.

"Can you tell me what's happening," Gabriel said, and his voice was tight, the way it got when he was trying to hold onto something -- control, composure, the role of the person who observes instead of the person who is acted upon. "I need to understand so I can tell people."

Arun looked at him. Then he looked at Elena. He made a decision that had nothing to do with protocol.

"Gabriel, listen." Arun's voice was quick, precise, and carried the urgency of someone who knew he was speaking during minutes that would be the most important of the colony's second year. "Fire in an open environment -- on Earth, in a field -- fire burns what it can reach and dies when it runs out of fuel or when the weather changes. The smoke goes up. It disperses. The air is replaced by millions of cubic meters of clean atmosphere. The fire is dangerous because of heat and speed."

He pointed at the bulkhead, at the gray smoke leaking through the seams.

"This is different. This is a sealed habitat. The air in there is not being replaced by fresh atmosphere because there is no fresh atmosphere. What's out there is vacuum and carbon dioxide. What's in there is one hundred eighty cubic meters of nitrogen-oxygen mix that we made, we purified, we breathed, and now it is feeding a fire that is consuming it molecule by molecule. The smoke is not dispersing. It is accumulating. Every cubic centimeter of air in that habitat is becoming poison."

Gabriel nodded. He was already processing, translating, understanding.

"Smoke is a suspension of particles -- solid carbon, unburned hydrocarbons, microscopic pieces of everything the fire has consumed. But smoke in a sealed space is not just particles. It's chemistry. Plastics burning produce carbon monoxide, hydrogen cyanide, phosgene, hydrochloric acid. Every material in Habitat Three -- the wall panels, the wiring insulation, the furniture, the clothing, the bedding -- all of it is synthetic. All of it is a fuel. All of it is becoming something that people cannot breathe."

Arun continued, faster now. "And pressure is part of the problem. Fire needs oxygen to burn. The fire is consuming oxygen, yes -- but the combustion is also heating the air, expanding it, raising the pressure. If the pressure rises too fast, seals fail. If seals fail, the pressure wave carries smoke into every compartment the bulkheads don't isolate perfectly. And nothing is perfectly isolated. Nothing."

Gabriel understood. The explanation was landing with the heavy clarity of a truth he had known intellectually but never felt viscerally. On Earth, fire killed by consuming the fuel of a single structure. Here, fire killed by transforming the entire atmosphere into an enemy.

"What about suppression," Gabriel asked.

Arun's expression answered before his words did. "The water mist system in Habitat Three is designed for small electrical fires. Not this. Not a fire that started in a wall and has already reached furnishings. The water mist will help. But it won't stop it alone."

The environmental panel lit up with new data. Arun's eyes tracked multiple readings simultaneously.

"Temperature in Zone D common area is one hundred and twelve degrees Celsius. Smoke particulate concentration -- " he stopped. Read it again. "Eighteen thousand micrograms per cubic meter. That's beyond any measurement I expected to see in a living space. Carbon monoxide -- two hundred and forty parts per million. At four hundred ppm, exposure for one hour is fatal. We're halfway to lethal concentration in six minutes."

Gabriel felt the numbers land like weights. He looked at the bulkhead, at the smoke that was no longer gray but a deep, dirty yellow-brown, and he understood exactly what Arun had just told him.

The air in Habitat Three was becoming unbreathable. The smoke was becoming lethal. The pressure was rising. And the fire had not yet reached its peak.

"I need to tell the colony," Gabriel said. But he was not moving. His feet were planted and his hand on the bulkhead was vibrating with the sound of the fire beyond the metal.

Elena put her hand on his shoulder. "Go. Tell them. Then go back to people management. I need the humans calm and the humans moving and I cannot do both alone."

Gabriel turned and walked back toward the main habitat, breathing through his mask, carrying the worst kind of knowledge -- not just that they were in danger, but that the danger had physics, and chemistry, and momentum, and every second of delay made it worse.

---

## Scene 3

*Compartment sealing initiated,* Mission AI announced through the habitat's public address system, its voice calm and flat in a way that was almost worse than any alarm. *Bulkhead B7 between Connector Hall and Habitat Three is closing. Estimated seal time: twelve seconds. Bulkhead B8 between Habitat Three Zones A and B is closing. Estimated seal time: eleven seconds. All personnel not inside Habitat Three should clear immediate area.*

The sound of the bulkhead closing was heavy and mechanical -- motors driving steel plates into rubber-sealed tracks, the colony's primary defense against cascade failure. The bulkheads had been installed after the blackout of Station Day 473, when Mission AI and Arun had redesigned the base around compartment independence and graceful failure. Every sealed space could be isolated from every other sealed space. A fire in one zone would not become a fire in the base.

In theory.

Bulkhead B7 closed at 03:24. The seal held. Smoke continued to leak through microscopic gaps -- no seal was perfect under pressure -- but the main flow was stopped. Elena verified seal integrity on her tablet: green. Holding.

"Bulkhead B7 sealed," Elena reported. "Arun, what about internal Habitat Three bulkheads. Can we isolate Zone D."

B7 sealed. Atmosphere isolation confirmed. Habitat Three internal bulkheads are controlled locally. I am attempting to activate Zone D isolation. The internal panel in Habitat Three is responding to commands. Bulkhead between Zone C and Zone D is partially closed. Eighty percent sealed. The remaining gap -- "

"What's preventing full closure." Elena's voice was level. Elena's voice was always level, even when nothing about the situation deserved levelness.

"Thermal expansion. The fire has heated the bulkhead frame. The metal has expanded approximately two millimeters. The gap cannot close completely."

Two millimeters. In a fire, two millimeters was a canyon.

"Robots," Elena said. "Tomas. Where are they."

Tomas was at her side. He had not been running. Tomas had walked -- the walk of someone moving through muscle memory, the kind of movement that comes from years of commanding machines that cannot panic and do not need reassurance.

"Four units are at the Habitat Three airlock. Entering now. Suppression mode confirmed. They carry water mist canisters and thermal imaging."

The first robot entered Habitat Three at 03:26.

Elena watched through the thermal camera feed that Tomas had patched to her tablet. The image was grainy, processed through smoke and heat, but it told a story that was worse than anything the naked eye could see.

The thermal image showed the fire in Zone D as a concentrated orange-red bloom on the western wall -- exactly where Arun had found the degraded insulation. The wire bundle had failed. The temporary tape had not been enough. The arc had ignited the wall paneling, and the fire had spread upward, following the vertical conduits, reaching the common area ceiling where synthetic acoustic panels and insulation caught like kindling.

The fire had a clear front -- it was burning along the western wall and advancing toward the center of the room. Temperature at the fire front: 240 degrees Celsius. The center of the common area was 160 degrees. The eastern side, the side facing the unsealed bulkhead to Zone C, was 90 degrees and climbing.

"First robot is engaging," Tomas reported.

Through the video feed, Elena watched the humanoid robot raise its suppression cannon and fire a water mist into the heart of the blaze. The mist hit the fire front. Steam exploded outward, momentarily obscuring the thermal camera. The temperature reading dropped: 200. 178. 165.

But it climbed back. 192. 211.

"It's not enough," Arun said from behind her. He had been watching the same feed, running his own calculations in his head. "That fire has too much fuel. The wall panels are aluminum-honeycomb composite with polymer facing -- they burn hot and they burn deep. Water mist cools the surface but the heat is already inside the material. It's like trying to put out a campfire with a spray bottle."

"Second robot entering," Tomas said.

The second robot carried a different load -- foam suppressant, designed for fuel fires, not recommended for electrical environments. But the electrical had already been cut to Habitat Three. There was nothing left to shock.

"Deploying foam."

On the thermal camera, the foam appeared as a cold blue-white spread across the fire front. The temperature dropped more significantly this time: 145. 128. 112.

It held at 112 for twelve seconds. Then it climbed again: 119. 131. 147.

"The fire is adapting," Arun said, and the word was not metaphorical to him. Fire did not think. But it behaved in ways that resembled strategy -- finding new fuel, exploiting new pathways, moving toward oxygen where it was available. "It's burning through the foam. It's reaching the acoustic panels in the ceiling. Those are polyurethane. They burn at 370 degrees and produce cyanide."

Elena's jaw tightened. "How much time."

"Before what. Before the fire reaches a critical mass where no suppression will work. Before the oxygen drops enough that the fire self-extinguishes. Before the smoke kills anyone trapped inside. Before the pressure compromises a bulkhead." Arun's voice had the flat precision of a man reciting data that he wished he was not reciting. "All of those clocks are running at the same time and I don't have clean answers for any of them."

"The robots can't hold it," Tomas said. He was not panicking. He was reporting. "They have limited suppressant. Approximately twelve minutes of continuous fire at this intensity. After that, they retreat and we need a new plan."

"Eleven minutes fifty seconds," Mission AI confirmed. "Robot Alpha-7 has expended forty-one percent of its water mist reserve. Robot Alpha-9 has expended thirty-three percent of its foam reserve. Both are operating at maximum duty cycle. Thermal stress on both units exceeds design parameters by twelve percent."

"Get them as much as they can give," Elena said. "And I'm going in."

"Elena -- " Arun started.

"I'm not going in blind. I'm going in with a third robot, a fresh load, and the bulkhead to Zone D at eighty percent. I'm going in because we are losing this fight from outside it and the only thing that stops a fire in a sealed habitat is removing its fuel faster than it can burn."

She was already moving toward the equipment bay, already pulling a fire suit off the rack. It was heavier than an EVA suit, designed for heat and toxic environment instead of vacuum and radiation.

"Elena," Laila's voice came from the corridor. She had positioned herself at the triage point, oxygen masks and burn treatment kits spread across a folding table. "If you go in there, you breathe whatever is in there that the suit doesn't filter. You know what the combustion products are. You know what cyanide does."

"I know."

"Then come back out before the sensors tell you to stay."

Elena looked at her. For a fraction of a second, the commander disappeared and the friend appeared -- the woman who had shared meals and arguments and sleepless nights and the kind of trust that only exists between people who have been responsible for each other's lives for seven years.

"I hear you," Elena said. She pulled the suit on. "I'm not planning to be a hero. I'm planning to buy time."

She stepped into the airlock at 03:30. The inner door cycled. The atmosphere inside was already hot and thick with smoke despite the robot ventilation. She could taste it through her filters -- acrid, chemical, wrong.

The outer door opened. She entered Habitat Three, and the heat hit her like a wall.

---

## Scene 4

Jonah was in the fabrication bay when the alarm went off. He did not run. He walked -- the deliberate walk of a man who had spent seven years understanding that running on Mars, on a tilting surface in artificial gravity, was how injuries happened.

But once the walk got him to the equipment bay, his hands moved with a speed that nothing on Mars could slow.

He pulled a fire suppression kit from its rack -- a modified unit he had built himself two years ago after the blackout, when he had realized that the imported fire systems were designed for Earth-class fires and Earth-class response times. His kit was heavier. It carried more suppressant. And it had a nozzle design that produced a wider, denser mist pattern than the standard equipment.

He was about to move toward Habitat Three when Arun grabbed his arm.

"Don't go in. Elena is going in with the robots. I need you here."

Jonah stopped. Looking. "What do you need."

"The bulkhead between Zone C and Zone D is stuck at eighty percent. Thermal expansion. I need a mechanical solution. Can you wedge it shut from the outside."

Jonah's expression changed from the general readiness of the fire response to the specific intensity of a fabrication problem. This was his language. This was what he knew -- not emergency protocols or command structures or medical triage, but the physics of materials under stress, the geometry of gaps, the difference between a tool that was designed for a job and a tool that could do a job despite never being asked.

"I need a thermal wedge and a lever. And I need something that won't melt at hundred-degree temperatures."

"Take the titanium spacer from the reactor maintenance kit," Arun said immediately.

They moved together toward Habitat Two's connector, taking the long route around the sealed bulkhead. They entered Habitat Three from the Zone A side -- the smoke was lighter here, gray but not opaque, the temperature elevated but not lethal.

Zone C was a different world.

Jonah stood at the bulkhead between Zone C and Zone D and saw the gap -- two millimeters of space that should have been sealed, and through that two millimeters he could see the glow. Not fire, not directly. But the light of intense heat bouncing off far walls, illuminating smoke that moved with the slow, purposeful flow of a river.

He could feel the heat radiating through the gap. It was like opening an oven door.

"The frame's expanding," Jonah said, pressing his hand to the bulkhead frame and pulling it back immediately. The metal was hot enough to feel like pain. "Maybe three, maybe four millimeters of thermal expansion across the whole frame. The gap is where the expansion is uneven."

He opened his kit. The titanium spacer was heavy, dense, and wouldn't soften until temperatures exceeded sixteen hundred degrees. He positioned it against the bulkhead edge where the gap was widest.

"I need more. The spacer covers maybe a third of the gap." He pulled a ceramic-fiber strip from his kit -- material normally used as gasket lining in the fabrication furnace. "This won't seal it. But it will reduce flow by maybe sixty percent if I can get it in there."

Arun watched him work. "You're trying to seal a two-millimeter gap with hand tools in a smoke-filled corridor while a fire burns on the other side."

"That's the job."

Jonah worked for four minutes. His hands were steady. The spacer went in first, positioned at the widest point of the gap. The ceramic strip followed, pushed into the remaining space with a flat driver, compressed until it filled what it could. He used a third piece -- a strip of salvaged ablative material from a heat shield, flexible enough to conform to the irregular gap but fire-resistant enough to survive contact with superheated air.

"I'm going to try the lever," he said. "I need to compress the frame slightly -- just enough to close what I can't fill."

He positioned a titanium pry bar against the bulkhead frame and applied force. The metal groaned. The gap narrowed: two millimeters. One point five. One.

Then the spacer cracked.

Jonah heard it before he saw it -- a sharp, high-frequency crack that he immediately recognized as material failure. He pulled back. The titanium spacer, a component he had fabricated from recycled titanium ingot six months ago, had developed a hairline fracture under thermal stress and pressure. It split with a second crack and fell away from the bulkhead.

The gap reopened.

"Damn it," Jonah said, and his voice was not loud but it carried the particular weight of a failure that was also a personal indictment.

He had made that part. He knew its specifications. He had tested it for mechanical loads. He had not tested it for thermal cycling under fire conditions because no one had anticipated that scenario. He had been confident. He had been wrong.

"Don't blame yourself for a problem nobody prepared for," Arun said. "Try the ceramic."

"The ceramic alone won't hold the gap against the frame expansion. I have too big a gap."

Jonah's mind was already working through the options, discarding what wouldn't work, iterating on what might. The spacer was gone. The ceramic was too soft. He had the heat shield material, but it was thin -- a millimeter at most.

Then he looked at the door frame itself.

"Arun. The rubber seal on the bulkhead. It's rated to two hundred degrees. What temperature is the frame."

Arun checked his thermal reader. "Frame surface: one hundred and eighty degrees. Rising."

"Forty-degree buffer. The rubber is still functional." Jonah pressed his gloved hand to the bulkhead seal ring. It was warm but not hot enough to be degrading. "If I can push the bulkhead another millimeter, the rubber seal will compress enough to close the gap without the spacer."

He repositioned the pry bar. Applied force more carefully this time -- not against the spacer, but directly against the bulkhead, using the frame as a fulcrrum.

The metal groaned. The frame moved -- barely. A fraction of a millimeter. But it was enough. The rubber seal compressed. The ceramic strip filled what remained. The heat shield ablative material conformed to the smallest irregularities.

Jonah held the bar for ten seconds, feeling the bulkhead, listening for the sound of escaping air.

There was none.

He released the bar slowly. The frame held. The seal held.

He looked at the broken titanium spacer on the floor -- his own fabrication, fractured by conditions it was never supposed to face -- and then at the sealed bulkhead, where the rubber seal he had not fabricated but simply understood well enough to use correctly was holding against a fire that was actively trying to breach it.

One locally made component failed.

One held.

Jonah picked up the broken spacer and put it in his pocket. He would examine it later. He would learn from it. But for now, he had a fire to fight.

"Seal is holding," he told Arun. "Sixty, maybe seventy percent reduction in smoke flow. It's not perfect."

"It's more than perfect is doing right now," Arun said. He checked his thermal reader. "Zone C temperature holding at ninety-two degrees. Not climbing. The seal is working."

Jonah nodded. "What's next."

Arun looked toward the sound of the fire -- a low, continuous roar that was audible even through the bulkheads and the mask and the mechanical hum of ventilation trying to clear what it could.

"Next we wait and see if the robots and Elena can finish what your seal just made possible."

---

## Scene 5

Elena was inside Zone D.

The world had narrowed to the radius of her vision, the reach of her arms, and the capacity of the air in her lungs. The fire suit protected her from heat and flame, but it did not protect her from the psychological effect of being inside a room that was actively becoming a hostile environment.

The thermal camera on her helmet showed the fire as a shifting landscape of color -- deep red at the edges, yellow-orange at the core, white-hot where it had found concentrated fuel. The room was unrecognizable. The common area where six people ate, where children had played on the floor, where the walls had held photographs and schedules and a hand-drawn map of Mars that Sana had made during the first year -- all of it was obscured by smoke and flame.

Her robot was beside her, firing water mist into the fire front. The steam was thick, blinding, reducing visibility to zero. She was navigating by the thermal feed alone.

"Arun," she said over the comms. Her voice was distorted by the mask and the ambient noise of the fire. "Status on the seal."

"Jonah sealed the Zone C bulkhead manually. Sixty to seventy percent reduction in flow. Zone C temperature is holding."

"Good. That's good. I'm pushing the fire back from the western wall. But the ceiling acoustic panels are still burning. They're producing -- " she coughed, tasted chemicals through the filter " -- I can't tell you what they're producing but the smoke is thick and the air tastes wrong."

"Cyanide risk is extreme," Laila's voice, cutting in from her position at the triage station. "Elena, how long have you been inside."

"Seven minutes."

"Your filters are rated for fifteen at this concentration. You have eight minutes. Make them count."

Elena did not argue. She directed the robot to concentrate on the ceiling panels, where the fire was spreading along the polyurethane insulation. The water hit the panels. Steam rose. Panels fell, charred and smoking, from the ceiling. The fire front retreated by half a meter.

Then it stopped retreating.

The fire was reaching something new -- a storage cabinet against the eastern wall, partially insulated by distance from the main blaze. The cabinet contained fabric supplies, spare clothing bedsheets. The heat had been enough to reach the autoignition temperature of the cotton-polyester blend.

The cabinet caught fire.

"New ignition," Elena reported. "Eastern wall. Cabinet with textiles."

"Second robot, redirect to eastern wall," Tomas ordered the machines.

Through the comms, Elena heard the robot's hydraulic actuators whine as it turned. But she also heard something else -- a low, deep sound, like a sigh.

"Arun, what was that."

A pause. "Pressure monitoring. Zone D internal pressure just peaked. Two point one atmospheres. It was two point two. The fire heated the air, the air expanded, the pressure rose. Now it's dropping."

"Is that good."

"It means the fire is consuming oxygen faster than the heat is expanding the remaining air. Oxygen concentration in Zone D is down to thirteen percent. At ten percent, the fire begins to self-suffocate."

"How long to ten percent."

"Four to six minutes based on current consumption rate. But the fire is finding new fuel paths. Every new material it reaches restarts the oxygen draw and adds new smoke production." Arun paused. "This is a race between the fire running out of oxygen and the fire finding enough fuel to last longer than the oxygen will."

Elena stared at the fire front. The water mist was cooling the surface but the heat was still deep in the materials. The newly ignited cabinet was adding to the oxygen demand.

"Jonah's seal is holding," Arun continued. "Without it, Zone C would have flashover in approximately four minutes. With it, Zone C is holding. That's the difference between a contained fire and a colony fire. He bought us time."

Elena did not respond. She was redirecting her robot's aim at the cabinet, adding her own supplemental spray from the hand-held extinguisher she'd carried in -- a CO2 unit for concentrated spot suppression. The blast hit the cabinet door. The fire inside wavered.

"Three minutes left on your filters," Laila reminded her.

"I see it."

Two hundred and forty seconds. She directed the robot to saturate the cabinet while she moved to the western wall, where the original fire had started. If she could collapse the remaining fuel there -- break apart the burning wall paneling, expose the non-combustible structural studs behind it -- she might deprive the fire of something to bridge to.

She used the pry bar on her belt to pull the burning paneling away from the wall. The material crumbled, blackened, hot enough to glow through the smoke. She kicked it toward the center of the room where the water mist from the robot was thickest.

"One minute," Arun said. "Oxygen is down to eleven percent. The fire is slowing but not stopping."

"Fifty seconds on your filter," Laila said.

Elena pulled one more panel loose. Then another. The exposed wall behind them was bare structural aluminum -- not a fuel source, not a conductor of heat to anything further. She had created a firebreak.

"Thirty seconds, Elena," Laila said. Her voice had no edge of command -- only the edge of medicine, of someone who knew exactly what chemical compounds were in that smoke and exactly what would happen if Elena breathed them.

"Done," Elena said. She was moving toward the exit, the robot following, still firing mist to keep the fire from reclaiming the fuel she had just exposed.

"Oxygen at ten point five percent," Arun reported. "Fire is self-limiting. It's not out but it's dying. The rate of spread is dropping."

Elena reached the bulkhead at 03:44. She cycled it through the airlock. The smoke was thick in the corridor, but it was the gray of exhausted combustion, not the yellow-brown of active fire.

She stepped into the corridor and someone -- Tomas -- pulled her mask off and guided her toward clean air. She gasped, filling her lungs with air that tasted like nothing, which was the most delicious thing she had ever tasted.

The bulkhead to Zone D sealed behind her with a final, heavy thud.

Through the thermal feed, watched one by one on Arun's tablet, the fire zone slowly dimmed. Orange faded to dull red. Red faded to dark. Not extinguished -- embers still glowed in the wreckage of the common area. But contained. No longer advancing. No longer consuming.

The colony had survived the first minutes of the fire.

Not the damage. Not the smoke already spread into three compartments. Not the structural inspection that would take days and the psychological aftermath that would take years. But the fire was contained. The bulkheads had held. The compartmentalization that Elena had ordered after the blackout had worked exactly as designed.

Arun sat on a crate in the corridor, his tablet dark in his hands, finally allowing his shoulders to drop from the rigid tension of the last twenty-seven minutes. Jonah stood beside him, still holding the pry bar, his fire-stained hands resting against thighs that were shaking with adrenaline he had not noticed until the shaking started.

Jonah looked at the broken titanium spacer on the floor beside him — the part he had made, the part that had failed — and then at the sealed bulkhead, where the rubber seal and ceramic strip and heat shield material had done what the expensive imported components had been designed to do and hadn't.

Mei arrived at the corridor, having sealed the greenhouse and then walked the long route around the sealed bulkheads to reach them. She looked at the smoke residue on the walls, at the fire suits laid out for decontamination, at Elena sitting on the floor breathing clean air with her eyes closed.

Tomas recalled his robots. Both units had exceeded their thermal operating limits, and one had a damaged hand actuator from the pry bar work against superheated metal. They limped back through the bulkheads like soldiers returning from a fight they had barely survived.

Laila remained at the triage station, her oxygen masks unused — not because no one needed them, but because the robot ventilation in the connector hall had cleared the worst of the smoke before it could reach the people standing in it. Sana was behind her in the medbay, still breathing clean air, still safe, still carrying the future through the present disaster.

Gabriel was writing. Not on a terminal — the terminals in the connector were offline — but on paper, with a pen, because some things needed to be recorded in the oldest way and the most durable way. His notes were brief, factual, stripped of everything except the sequence of events:

*03:17 — Alarm. First colony fire emergency. Zone D, Habitat Three. Cause: electrical ignition at compromised wire junction.*
*03:19 — Main ventilation isolated. Robots deployed. Bulkhead B7 closing.*
*03:24 — Bulkhead B7 sealed. Interior bulkhead between Zones C and D stuck at 80% — thermal expansion.*
*03:26 — Robots engaged with water mist and foam suppressant. Fire advancing along ceiling panels.*
*03:30 — Commander entered Zone D with robot support.*
*03:32 — Manual seal of Zone C/D bulkhead by fabrication chief using titanium spacer, ceramic fiber, heat shield material. Spacer failed — locally fabricated titanium fracture under thermal stress. Seal held using rubber gasket and manual wedge.*
*03:38 — New ignition at eastern storage cabinet. Oxygen dropping.*
*03:44 — Commander exited Zone D. Fire self-limiting at 10.5% oxygen. Contained.*
*27 minutes from ignition to containment. No casualties. One robot damaged. Extensive habitat damage in Zone D.*

He closed the notebook. His hand was steadier than it had been.

Elena stood. She looked at the people in the corridor — soot-stained, exhausted, breathing hard. She looked at the sealed bulkheads. She looked at the smoke residue on every surface.

"Nobody goes back in until Arun clears it for atmosphere and structure. We run air scrubbers in the connector for the next six hours. All non-essential power stays off in Habitat Three. Laila — everyone who was in the smoke gets checked, even if they feel fine. I want carbon monoxide blood levels on the entire zone."

She paused. The command voice was still holding. It had to hold a little longer.

"Good work," she said. Not loud. Not emotional. But real. "Everybody did good work. Now rest. We need to be ready for tomorrow."

But as people began to disperse, moving through the smoke-stained corridors toward their quarters and their beds in a habitat that no longer felt entirely safe, Arun stood at the environmental monitoring station and read the numbers that told the next part of the story.

Zone D was contained but uninhabitable. Zone C had been exposed to elevated smoke and temperature. Zone B was clear but isolated, its residents displaced into a base that was already running tight on space and power. The air scrubbers would need to run for days. The structural inspection would reveal damage that no one could yet quantify.

The colony had survived twenty-seven minutes of fire.

Now came the hours. Now came the days. Now came the question of whether twenty years of learning — seven of them on this planet, the rest before that in simulations and training and engineering on Earth — was enough to hold the next emergency, the one that was already forming in the gaps between what they had survived and what they had to fix.

Containment became a test of twenty years of learning.

---

Oxygen in Zone D is at 9.8 percent and declining — the fire is consuming what remains at a decreasing rate. Smoke particulate concentration in the connector hall has dropped from a peak of 12,400 micrograms per cubic meter to 890. The air scrubbers are operating at maximum capacity. I estimate the connector hall will be clear of visible airborne smoke in approximately four hours. The connector hall will require chemical decontamination for surface residues. I am tracking the following: structural integrity of Zone D -- cannot be assessed until atmosphere is safe for inspection. Damage to imported wall panels -- approximately eighty percent of Zone D western wall and ceiling panels are structurally compromised. Damage to locally fabricated components -- one titanium spacer failed under thermal stress. Failure mode: hairline fracture initiated during fabrication, propagated under load. I have added this to the quality assurance database as a new entry: Fabricated Component 447 -- Thermal Stress Failure Under Fire Conditions. This is the first fire-related component failure in colony history. It will not be the last lesson. I am also monitoring Sana's vital signs in the medbay. They have remained stable throughout the event. Heart rate elevated at the peak of the alarm. Blood pressure within normal range. Oxygen saturation at 99 percent. The pregnancy continues unaffected by the fire. I am recording this as well. The data will matter later -- to the medical archive, to the historical record, to the future inhabitants of this colony who will ask what the first fire on Mars was like and whether it changed the way we built things. It did. It already has. It changed how Jonah fabricates parts. It changed how Arun thinks about fire suppression. It changed how Elena thinks about compartment isolation and response times. It changed how Laila measures risk. It changed how Gabriel records events. I am not the only one who has been changed by this fire. The colony is different now. It still exists. It still breathes.
