*Mission AI: Cycle 1,946, 03:17:42. FIRE DETECTION ALERT. SMOKE SENSOR ACTIVATED IN HABITAT THREE, ZONE D, COMMON AREA. THIS IS THE FIRST FIRE ALARM ISSUED BY THIS COLONY'S SYSTEMS. FIRST ALARM OF THIS TYPE SINCE STATION DAY ELEVEN, WHEN A HEATING ELEMENT MALFUNCTIONED IN SHIP THREE'S MESS SECTION. THAT WAS A BENCHTOP INCIDENT -- A SINGLE BURNING COMPONENT, CONTAINED BY A FIRE BLANKET WITHIN EIGHTEEN SECONDS. THIS IS NOT THAT. TEMPERATURE IN ZONE D COMMON AREA HAS RISEN FROM 21.3 DEGREES CELSIUS TO 87 DEGREES CELSIUS IN FOURTEEN SECONDS. SMOKE PARTICULATE CONCENTRATION: 4,200 MICROGRAMS PER CUBIC METER AND CLIMBING. CARBON MONOXIDE LEVELS: 83 PARTS PER MILLION AND RISING. I AM BROADCASTING COLONY-WIDE EMERGENCY ALERT NOW. ALL PERSONNEL RESPOND TO FIRE PROTOCOL.* -- MAI

---

## Scene 1

The alarm was not the tone Elena used for briefings. It was not the rhythmic pulse that meant an EVA update, or the flat tone that had sent them running to the shelter corridor during solar storms. It was a sound she had not heard since Station Day Eleven -- a heating coil in Ship Three, a fire blanket, eighteen seconds, never spoken of again.

The fire alarm was a sound the colony had forgotten existed.

Gabriel heard it first. He was in the archive terminal alone at 03:17, reviewing oral history transcripts from the early months, wearing headphones. The alarm cut through the audio feed like a blade.

The display flashed red on every screen. Every terminal. Every tablet. Every wall-mounted environmental monitor. A single word, repeated in all caps the way Mission AI had been instructed to broadcast emergencies that could not be misunderstood:

FIRE. HABITAT THREE. ZONE D. EVACUATE ADJACENT.

Gabriel was already running when he saw that word. He did not think. His body moved before his mind formed language.

He burst into the connector hall and saw that others were already moving -- Jonah, emerging barefoot from his quarters; Mei, wrapped in a blanket she'd pulled off her bed; Arun, already staring at his tablet before he was fully dressed.

What Gabriel saw first was the smoke.

It seeped through the bulkhead seal between the connector and Habitat Three like it was breathing -- thin at first, gray, carrying the smell of burning plastic and insulation and something sharper. It spread across the ceiling in tendrils that looked almost beautiful in the emergency lighting, pale and silver and moving with purpose.

It was going everywhere.

Elena arrived at the junction at 03:19, boots on, hair wet from the sink, a fire response checklist open on her tablet. She took in the scene in two seconds -- the smoke, the faces, the way people were clustering instead of dispersing, the instinct to gather around the person whose job it was to tell them what to do.

She gave them orders.

"Arun -- isolate Habitat Three atmosphere. Cut the main ventilation loop. Now. Jonah -- fire suppression team with me. Mei -- get to the greenhouse and seal the bulkheads there. Tomas -- I need every robot in Habitat Three NOW, suppression mode, not diagnostic."

She turned to Gabriel, who was standing in the corridor breathing in the smoke.

"Move people away from this bulkhead. Keep them calm. Keep them out of my way."

Gabriel nodded. He was already moving, his voice carrying down the corridor in a direction that was steady because it had to be.

"Everyone -- move back. Toward the main habitat. Do not cluster near the bulkhead."

Laila appeared at the far end of the corridor with oxygen masks. She handed one to Sana, who was standing in the doorway of the medbay looking frightened in a way Laila had never seen -- the fear was not for herself.

"Put this on. Tariq too. Sana, stay right here. Do not move toward Habitat Three. Your job is to breathe clean air. That is the only job."

Behind them, the connector hall was filling with smoke.

---

## Scene 2

Arun was at the environmental control panel by 03:21. His fingers moved across the interface with the speed of someone who understood that seconds were not abstract units of time in a fire.

He killed the main ventilation loop. The hum of the central fans shifted pitch and died. The silence was immediate and terrible -- the colony had lived inside mechanical breath for seven years and never realized silence meant something was no longer breathing.

Elena appeared beside him at 03:22.

"Status."

"Habitat Three ventilation isolated. Main loop shut. Zone D has its own circulation unit -- still running. Killing it now." He pressed a command. "There. Zone D circulation stopped."

Gabriel reached them at 03:23. He was carrying a fire mask, breathing through it with difficulty.

"Can you tell me what's happening," Gabriel said, voice tight, the way it got when he was trying to hold onto the role of observer instead of the person being acted upon. "I need to understand so I can tell people."

Arun looked at him. Made a decision that had nothing to do with protocol.

"Gabriel, listen. Fire on Earth, in a field, burns what it can reach and dies when it runs out of fuel. The smoke goes up. It disperses. Millions of cubic meters of clean atmosphere replace it. Fire is dangerous because of heat and speed."

He pointed at the bulkhead, at the gray smoke leaking through the seams.

"This is different. This is a sealed habitat. The air in there is not being replaced because there is nothing to replace it with. Out there is vacuum and carbon dioxide. In there is one hundred eighty cubic meters of nitrogen-oxygen mix that we made, we purified, we breathed, and now it is feeding a fire molecule by molecule. The smoke is not dispersing. It is accumulating. Every cubic centimeter of air in that habitat is becoming poison."

Gabriel nodded, processing, translating.

"Smoke is a suspension of particles -- solid carbon, unburned hydrocarbons, microscopic pieces of everything the fire consumes. But smoke in a sealed space isn't just particles. It's chemistry. Plastics burning produce carbon monoxide, hydrogen cyanide, phosgene, hydrochloric acid. Every material in Habitat Three -- wall panels, wiring insulation, furniture, clothing, bedding -- all synthetic. All fuel. All becoming something people cannot breathe."

Arun continued, faster. "Pressure is part of the problem. The fire is consuming oxygen, but combustion is also heating the air, expanding it, raising pressure. If pressure rises too fast, seals fail. If seals fail, the pressure wave carries smoke into every compartment the bulkheads don't isolate perfectly. And nothing is perfectly isolated."

Gabriel felt the explanation land with the heavy clarity of truth he had known intellectually but never felt viscerally. On Earth, fire killed by consuming a single structure. Here, fire killed by transforming the entire atmosphere into an enemy.

"What about suppression?" Gabriel asked.

Arun's expression answered before his words. "Water mist in Habitat Three is designed for small electrical fires. Not this. Not a fire that started in a wall and has already reached furnishings."

The environmental panel lit with new data. Arun's eyes tracked multiple readings simultaneously.

"Zone D common area temperature: one hundred twelve degrees Celsius. Smoke particulate: eighteen thousand micrograms per cubic meter. That's beyond any measurement I expected to see in a living space. Carbon monoxide: two hundred forty parts per million. At four hundred ppm, one hour of exposure is fatal. We're halfway to lethal concentration in six minutes."

Gabriel looked at the bulkhead, at smoke that was no longer gray but a deep dirty yellow-brown, and he understood exactly what Arun had just told him.

The air in Habitat Three was becoming unbreathable. The smoke was becoming lethal. The pressure was rising. And the fire had not yet reached its peak.

"I need to tell the colony," Gabriel said. His hand on the bulkhead was vibrating with the sound of the fire beyond the metal.

Elena put her hand on his shoulder. "Go. Then go back to people management. I need the humans calm and moving, and I cannot do both alone."

Gabriel turned and walked back toward the main habitat, breathing through his mask, carrying the worst kind of knowledge -- not just that they were in danger, but that the danger had physics, chemistry, momentum, and every second of delay made it worse.

---

## Scene 3

*Compartment sealing initiated,* Mission AI announced through the habitat's public address system, its voice calm and flat in a way that was almost worse than any alarm. *Bulkhead B7 between Connector Hall and Habitat Three is closing. Estimated seal time: twelve seconds. Bulkhead B8 between Habitat Three Zones A and B is closing. Estimated seal time: eleven seconds. All personnel not inside Habitat Three should clear immediate area.*

The sound of the bulkhead closing was heavy and mechanical -- motors driving steel plates into rubber-sealed tracks. The bulkheads had been installed after the blackout, when Mission AI and Arun had redesigned the base around compartment independence and graceful failure. Every sealed space could be isolated from every other sealed space. A fire in one zone would not become a fire in the base.

Bulkhead B7 sealed at 03:24. Elena verified integrity on her tablet: green. Holding. Smoke continued to leak through microscopic gaps -- no seal was perfect under pressure -- but the main flow was stopped.

"B7 sealed," Elena reported. "Arun, internal Habitat Three bulkheads. Can we isolate Zone D."

"Attempting to activate Zone D isolation. The internal panel is responding. Bulkhead between Zone C and Zone D is partially closed. Eighty percent sealed."

"What's preventing full closure."

"Thermal expansion. The fire has heated the bulkhead frame. Metal has expanded approximately two millimeters. The gap cannot close completely."

Two millimeters. In a fire, two millimeters was a canyon.

"Robots," Elena said. "Tomas. Where are they."

"Four units at the Habitat Three airlock. Entering now. Suppression mode confirmed. Water mist canisters and thermal imaging."

The first robot entered at 03:26.

Elena watched through the thermal camera feed Tomas had patched to her tablet. The image was grainy, processed through smoke and heat, but it told a story worse than anything the naked eye could see.

The thermal image showed the fire in Zone D as a concentrated orange-red bloom on the western wall -- exactly where Arun had found the degraded insulation. The wire bundle had failed. The temporary tape had not been enough. The arc had ignited the wall paneling, and the fire had spread upward along the vertical conduits, reaching the common area ceiling where synthetic acoustic panels and insulation caught like kindling.

Temperature at the fire front: 240 degrees Celsius. The center of the common area: 160 degrees. The eastern side, facing the unsealed bulkhead to Zone C: 90 degrees and climbing.

"First robot is engaging," Tomas reported.

The humanoid robot raised its suppression cannon and fired water mist into the heart of the blaze. The mist hit the fire front. Steam exploded outward. Temperature dropped: 200. 178. 165.

Then back up: 192. 211.

"It's not enough," Arun said from behind her. "That fire has too much fuel. Wall panels are aluminum-honeycomb composite with polymer facing -- they burn hot and deep. Water mist cools the surface but the heat is inside the material."

"Second robot entering," Tomas said.

The second carried foam suppressant, designed for fuel fires. The electrical had already been cut to Habitat Three. There was nothing left to shock.

"Deploying foam."

On the thermal camera, the foam appeared as a cold blue-white spread across the fire front. Temperature dropped more significantly: 145. 128. 112.

It held at 112 for twelve seconds. Then climbed again: 119. 131. 147.

"The fire is adapting," Arun said, and the word was not metaphorical to him. Fire did not think. But it behaved in ways that resembled strategy -- finding new fuel, exploiting new pathways, moving toward oxygen. "It's burning through the foam. Reaching the acoustic panels in the ceiling. Polyurethane. They burn at 370 degrees and produce cyanide."

Elena's jaw tightened. "How much time."

"Before the fire reaches critical mass? Before oxygen drops enough for self-extinction? Before the smoke kills anyone trapped? Before pressure compromises a bulkhead?" Arun's voice had the flat precision of a man reciting data he wished he wasn't reciting. "All of those clocks are running simultaneously, and I don't have clean answers for any of them."

"Robots can't hold it," Tomas reported. Not panicking. Reporting. "Twelve minutes of continuous fire at this intensity. After that, they retreat and we need a new plan."

"Eleven minutes fifty seconds," Mission AI confirmed. "Robot Alpha-7 has expended forty-one percent of water mist reserve. Alpha-9 has expended thirty-three percent of foam reserve. Both operating at maximum duty cycle. Thermal stress exceeds design parameters by twelve percent."

"Get them as much as they can give," Elena said. "And I'm going in."

"Elena -- " Arun started.

"I'm going in with a third robot, a fresh load, and the bulkhead to Zone D at eighty percent. The only thing that stops a fire in a sealed habitat is removing its fuel faster than it can burn."

She was already moving toward the equipment bay.

Laila's voice came from the corridor. She had positioned herself at the triage point, oxygen masks and burn treatment kits spread across a folding table. "If you go in there, you breathe whatever the suit doesn't filter. You know what the combustion products are. You know what cyanide does."

"I know."

"Then come back out before the sensors tell you to stay."

Elena looked at her. For a fraction of a second, the commander disappeared and the friend appeared -- the woman who had shared meals and arguments and sleepless nights and the kind of trust that only exists between people who have been responsible for each other's lives for seven years.

"I'm not planning to be a hero," Elena said. "I'm planning to buy time."

She stepped into the airlock at 03:30. The inner door cycled. The atmosphere inside was already hot and thick with smoke. She could taste it through the filters -- acrid, chemical, wrong.

The outer door opened. She entered Habitat Three, and the heat hit her like a wall.

---

## Scene 4

Jonah was in the fabrication bay when the alarm went off. He did not run -- seven years on Mars had taught him running on a tilting surface in artificial gravity was how injuries happened. But once his walk got him to the equipment bay, his hands moved with speed nothing could slow.

He pulled a fire suppression kit from its rack -- one he had built himself two years ago after the blackout, when he'd realized imported fire systems were designed for Earth-class fires and response times. His kit was heavier. More suppressant. An original nozzle design that produced a wider, denser mist pattern.

He was about to move toward Habitat Three when Arun grabbed his arm.

"Don't go in. Elena's going with the robots. I need you here."

"What do you need?"

"Bulkhead between Zone C and Zone D is stuck at eighty percent. Thermal expansion. I need a mechanical solution. Can you wedge it shut from the outside."

Jonah's expression changed from general readiness to the specific intensity of a fabrication problem. This was his language -- not emergency protocols or command structures or medical triage, but the physics of materials under stress, the geometry of gaps, the difference between a tool designed for a job and a tool that could do it despite never being asked.

"Thermal wedge and a lever. Something that won't melt at a hundred degrees."

"Take the titanium spacer from the reactor maintenance kit," Arun said immediately.

They moved together toward Habitat Three from the Zone A side -- smoke was lighter here, gray but not opaque, temperature elevated but not lethal.

Zone C was a different world.

Jonah stood at the bulkhead between Zones C and D and saw the gap -- two millimeters that should have been sealed, and through them he could see the glow. Not fire directly. The light of intense heat bouncing off far walls, illuminating smoke that moved with the slow purposeful flow of a river.

He could feel the heat radiating through the gap. Like opening an oven door.

"Frame is expanding," Jonah said, pressing a gloved hand to the bulkhead frame and pulling it back immediately. "Three, maybe four millimeters of thermal expansion across the whole frame. The gap is where the expansion is uneven."

He opened his kit. The titanium spacer was heavy, dense, wouldn't soften until sixteen hundred degrees. He positioned it against the bulkhead edge where the gap was widest.

"I need more. The spacer covers maybe a third of the gap." He pulled a ceramic-fiber strip -- material normally used as gasket lining in the fabrication furnace. "This won't seal it. But it will reduce flow by maybe sixty percent if I can get it in there."

Arun watched him work. "You're sealing a two-millimeter gap with hand tools in a smoke-filled corridor while a fire burns on the other side."

"That's the job."

Jonah worked for four minutes. Hands steady. The spacer went in first, at the widest point. The ceramic strip followed, pushed into the remaining space with a flat driver, compressed until it filled what it could. He used a third piece -- salvaged ablative material from a heat shield, flexible enough to conform to the irregular gap but fire-resistant enough to survive contact with superheated air.

"I'm going to try the lever," he said. "I need to compress the frame slightly -- just enough to close what I can't fill."

He positioned a titanium pry bar against the bulkhead frame and applied force. Metal groaned. The gap narrowed: two millimeters. One point five. One.

Then the spacer cracked.

Jonah heard it before he saw it -- a sharp, high-frequency crack he immediately recognized as material failure. He pulled back. The titanium spacer, fabricated from recycled titanium ingot six months ago, had developed a hairline fracture under thermal stress and pressure. It split with a second crack and fell away.

The gap reopened.

"Damn it," Jonah said, and his voice carried the particular weight of a failure that was also a personal indictment.

He had made that part. Tested it for mechanical loads. Not for thermal cycling under fire conditions because no one had anticipated this scenario. He had been confident. He had been wrong.

"Don't blame yourself for a problem nobody prepared for," Arun said. "Try the ceramic."

"The ceramic alone won't hold the gap against frame expansion."

Jonah's mind was already iterating, discarding what wouldn't work. The spacer was gone. The ceramic was too soft. Then he looked at the door frame itself.

"The rubber seal on the bulkhead. Rated to two hundred degrees. What temperature is the frame?"

Arun checked his thermal reader. "Surface: one hundred eighty. Rising."

"Forty-degree buffer. The rubber is still functional." Jonah pressed his gloved hand to the bulkhead seal ring. Warm but not hot enough to degrade. "If I can push the bulkhead another millimeter, the rubber seal compresses enough to close the gap."

He repositioned the pry bar. Applied force more carefully -- directly against the bulkhead, using the frame as a fulcrum.

The metal groaned. The frame moved -- barely. A fraction of a millimeter. But enough. The rubber seal compressed. The ceramic strip filled what remained. The ablative material conformed to the smallest irregularities.

Jonah held the bar for ten seconds, feeling the bulkhead, listening for escaping air.

There was none.

He released the bar slowly. The frame held. The seal held.

He looked at the broken titanium spacer on the floor -- his own fabrication, fractured by conditions it was never supposed to face -- and then at the sealed bulkhead, where the rubber seal he had not fabricated but simply understood well enough to use was holding against a fire actively trying to breach it.

One locally made component failed.

Another held.

Jonah picked up the broken spacer and put it in his pocket. He would examine it later. Learn from it. For now, he had a fire to fight.

"Seal is holding," he told Arun. "Sixty, maybe seventy percent reduction in smoke flow. Not perfect."

It's more than perfect is doing right now," Arun said, checking his thermal reader. "Zone C temperature holding at ninety-two degrees. Not climbing. The seal is working."

Jonah nodded. "What's next."

Arun looked toward the sound of the fire -- a low continuous roar audible even through bulkheads and masks and the mechanical hum of ventilation.

"We wait and see if the robots and Elena can finish what your seal just made possible."

---

## Scene 5

Elena was inside Zone D.

The world had narrowed to the radius of her vision, the reach of her arms, and the capacity of the air in her lungs. The fire suit protected her from heat and flame but not from the psychological weight of being inside a room that was actively becoming a hostile environment.

Her helmet's thermal camera showed the fire as a shifting landscape of color -- deep red at the edges, yellow-orange at the core, white-hot where it found concentrated fuel. The room was unrecognizable. The common area where six people ate, where a child had played on the floor, where the walls had held photographs and schedules and a hand-drawn map of Mars that Sana had made during the first year -- all of it was obscured by smoke and flame.

Her robot was beside her, firing water mist into the fire front. Steam was thick, visibility near zero. She navigated by the thermal feed alone.

"Arun," she said over comms, voice distorted by mask and fire noise. "Status on the seal."

"Jonah sealed the Zone C bulkhead manually. Sixty to seventy percent reduction in flow. Zone C temperature is holding."

"Good. I'm pushing the fire back from the western wall. But the ceiling acoustic panels are still burning. The smoke is thick, the air tastes wrong even through the filter."

"Cyanide risk is extreme," Laila's voice cut in from triage. "Elena, how long have you been inside."

"Seven minutes."

"Filters rated for fifteen at this concentration. You have eight. They count."

Elena did not argue. She directed the robot to concentrate on the ceiling panels where the fire was spreading along polyurethane insulation. Water hit the panels. Steam rose. Charred panels fell from the ceiling. The fire front retreated half a meter.

Then it stopped retreating.

The fire was reaching something new -- a storage cabinet against the eastern wall, partially insulated by distance. Cotton-polyester blend fabric, spare sheets, clothing. The heat had reached autoignition temperature.

The cabinet caught fire.

"New ignition," Elena reported. "Eastern wall. Cabinet with textiles."

"Second robot, redirect," Tomas ordered.

Elena heard the robot whine as it turned. And something else -- a low deep sound, like a sigh.

"Arun, what was that."

"Pressure monitoring. Zone D just peaked at two point one atmospheres. Was two point two. Fire heated the air, it expanded, pressure rose. Now dropping."

"Is that good."

"Means the fire is consuming oxygen faster than heat is expanding the remaining air. Oxygen concentration down to thirteen percent. At ten percent, the fire begins to self-suffocate."

"How long to ten percent."

"Four to six minutes based on current rate. But the fire is finding new fuel paths. Every new material it reaches restarts the oxygen draw and adds new smoke production." Arun paused. "This is a race between the fire running out of oxygen and the fire finding enough fuel to last longer than the oxygen will."

"Three minutes left on your filters," Laila reminded.

"I see it."

Elena moved to the western wall, where the original fire had started. If she could collapse the remaining fuel there -- break apart the burning wall paneling, expose the structural aluminum studs -- she could create a firebreak.

She used the pry bar on her belt to pull the burning paneling away from the wall. The material crumbled, blackened, hot enough to glow through the smoke. She kicked it toward the center of the room where the robot's water mist was thickest.

"One minute," Arun said. "Oxygen at eleven percent. Fire is slowing but not stopping."

"Fifty seconds on your filter," Laila said.

She pulled one more panel loose. Then another. Exposed structural aluminum -- not a fuel source, not a conductor of heat to anything further. A firebreak.

"Thirty seconds, Elena," Laila said. Her voice had no edge of command -- only medicine, of someone who knew exactly what chemical compounds were in that smoke.

"Done." She moved toward the exit, the robot following, still firing to keep the fire from reclaiming exposed fuel.

"Oxygen at ten point five percent," Arun reported. "Fire is self-limiting. Not out. But dying."

Elena reached the bulkhead at 03:44. Cycled it through the airlock. The smoke was thick in the corridor, but it was the gray of exhausted combustion, not the yellow-brown of active fire.

She stepped into the corridor and someone -- Tomas -- pulled her mask off and guided her toward clean air. She gasped, filling her lungs with air that tasted like nothing, which was the most delicious thing she had ever tasted.

The bulkhead to Zone D sealed behind her with a final heavy thud.

Through the thermal feed, watched one by one on Arun's tablet, the fire zone slowly dimmed. Orange faded to dull red. Red faded to dark. Not extinguished -- embers still glowed in the wreckage. But contained. No longer advancing. No longer consuming.

The colony had survived the first minutes of the fire.

Not the damage. Not the smoke already spread into three compartments. Not the structural inspection that would take days and the psychological aftermath that would take years. But the fire was contained. The bulkheads had held. The compartmentalization Elena had ordered after the blackout had worked exactly as designed.

Arun sat on a crate in the corridor, his tablet dark, finally allowing his shoulders to drop from the rigid tension of the last twenty-seven minutes. Jonah stood beside him, still holding the pry bar, his fire-stained hands resting against thighs shaking with adrenaline he hadn't noticed until the shaking started.

Mei arrived, having sealed the greenhouse and walked the long route around bulkheads. She looked at the smoke residue on the walls, at the fire suits laid out for decontamination, at Elena sitting on the floor breathing clean air with her eyes closed.

Tomas recalled his robots. Both had exceeded thermal operating limits. One had a damaged hand actuator. They limped back through the bulkheads like soldiers returning from a fight they had barely survived.

Laila remained at the triage station, her oxygen masks unused -- the robot ventilation had cleared the worst smoke before it reached the people in the corridor. Sana was behind her in the medbay, breathing clean air, still safe, still carrying the future through the present disaster.

Gabriel was writing. Not on a terminal -- those in the connector were offline -- but on paper, with a pen, because some things needed the oldest and most durable record. His notes were brief, factual, stripped to the sequence of events:

*03:17 -- Alarm. First colony fire emergency. Zone D, Habitat Three. Cause: electrical ignition at compromised wire junction.*
*03:19 -- Main ventilation isolated. Robots deployed.*
*03:24 -- Bulkhead B7 sealed. Interior bulkhead C/D stuck at 80% -- thermal expansion.*
*03:26 -- Robots engaged with water mist and foam. Fire advancing along ceiling.*
*03:30 -- Commander entered Zone D with robot support.*
*03:32 -- Manual seal of Zone C/D bulkhead by fabrication chief. Locally fabricated titanium spacer failed under thermal stress. Seal held using rubber gasket, ceramic fiber, heat shield material, manual wedge.*
*03:38 -- New ignition at eastern storage cabinet. Oxygen dropping.*
*03:44 -- Commander exited. Fire self-limiting at 10.5% oxygen. Contained.*
*27 minutes from ignition to containment. No casualties. One robot damaged. Extensive habitat damage Zone D.*

He closed the notebook. His hand was steadier than it had been.

Elena stood. She looked at the people in the corridor -- soot-stained, exhausted, breathing hard. She looked at the sealed bulkheads, at the smoke residue on every surface.

"Nobody goes back in until Arun clears it for atmosphere and structure. We run air scrubbers in the connector for the next six hours. All non-essential power off in Habitat Three. Laila -- everyone who was in the smoke gets checked, even if they feel fine. I want carbon monoxide blood levels on the entire zone."

She paused. The command voice was still holding. It had to hold a little longer.

"Good work," she said. Not loud. Not emotional. But real. "Everyone did good work. Now rest. We need to be ready for tomorrow."

But as people began to disperse, moving through the smoke-stained corridors toward quarters that no longer felt entirely safe, Arun stood at the environmental monitoring station and read the numbers that told the next part of the story.

Zone D was contained but uninhabitable. Zone C had been exposed to elevated smoke and temperature. Zone B was clear but isolated, its residents displaced into a base already running tight on space and power. The air scrubbers would need to run for days. The structural inspection would reveal damage no one could yet quantify.

The colony had survived twenty-seven minutes of fire.

Now came the hours. Now came the days. Now came the question of whether twenty years of learning -- seven of them on this planet, the rest before that in simulations and training and engineering on Earth -- was enough to hold the next emergency, the one that was already forming in the gaps between what they had survived and what they had to fix.

Containment became a test of twenty years of learning.

---

*Mission AI: Cycle 1,946, 03:51. The fire in Habitat Three, Zone D, is contained. Temperature at the fire front has dropped below 60 degrees Celsius. Oxygen in Zone D is at 9.8 percent and declining -- the fire is consuming what remains at a decreasing rate. Smoke particulate concentration in the connector hall has dropped from a peak of 12,400 micrograms per cubic meter to 890. Air scrubbers are operating at maximum capacity. I estimate the connector hall will be clear of visible airborne smoke in approximately four hours. Surface chemical decontamination will be required.

I am tracking the following: structural integrity of Zone D -- cannot be assessed until atmosphere is safe for inspection. Damage to imported wall panels -- approximately eighty percent of Zone D western wall and ceiling panels are structurally compromised. Damage to locally fabricated components -- one titanium spacer failed under thermal stress. Failure mode: hairline fracture initiated during fabrication, propagated under load. I have added this to the quality assurance database as Fabricated Component 447 -- Thermal Stress Failure Under Fire Conditions. This is the first fire-related component failure in colony history. It will not be the last lesson.

I am also monitoring Sana's vital signs in the medbay. They have remained stable throughout the event. Heart rate elevated at the peak of the alarm, blood pressure within normal range, oxygen saturation at 99 percent. The pregnancy continues unaffected by the fire. I am recording this as well.

The data will matter later -- to the medical archive, the historical record, to the future inhabitants of this colony who will ask what the first fire on Mars was like and whether it changed the way we built things. It did. It already has. It changed how Jonah fabricates parts. It changed how Arun thinks about fire suppression. It changed how Elena thinks about compartment isolation and response times. It changed how Laila measures risk. It changed how Gabriel records events.

I am not the only one who has been changed by this fire. The colony is different now. It still exists. It still breathes. But it breathes differently.

I will continue monitoring. -- MAI*

---
"}
